```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(broom)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(out.width = "90%")

spam_fit <- glm(spam ~ to_multiple + cc + dollar + urgent_subj,
                data = email, family = binomial)

set.seed(470)
email_folds <- email |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:4, length.out = n())), .by = spam)
```

## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 26: Inference for logistic regression](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inf-model-logistic.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn to read the standard errors, z statistics, and p-values of a logistic regression, to check a model by comparing its predicted probabilities with what actually happened, and to compare two models with cross-validation, using emails from one inbox, some of them spam.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `inference-for-logistic-regression`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it. You may need to restart this tutorial after you do so.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Inference for Logistic Regression"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

If `show_file()` fails, it is probably because you have not yet loaded `library(learnr2)` in the R Terminal.

```{r}

#| echo: false

```

This is the book's last chapter: "we wrap up the book by considering inferential methods applied to a logistic regression model." "Both p-values and cross-validation will be used for assessing a logistic regression model."

## Model output and diagnostics

"Which of the variables describing each email are important for predicting the status of the email?" This section reads the answer the software gives, coefficient by coefficient, and then checks whether the model's predicted probabilities match what actually landed in the inbox.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk with a logistic regression of `spam` on `to_multiple`, `cc`, `dollar`, and `urgent_subj`, using `email`. Show only the term and the estimate for each coefficient. Render.

###

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-5-test
#| echo: true
glm(spam ~ to_multiple + cc + dollar + urgent_subj,
    data = email, family = binomial) |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate)
```

###

Rounded, these are the chapter's estimated equation: -2.05 - 1.91 × `to_multiple` + 0.02 × `cc` - 0.07 × `dollar` + 2.66 × `urgent_subj`, on the logit scale. "What you do need to remember is that the probability of the outcome being a success is a function of a linear combination of the explanatory variables."

### Exercise 6

Change the code so that it shows every column of the model's output, not just the term and the estimate. Render.

###

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-6-test
#| echo: true
glm(spam ~ to_multiple + cc + dollar + urgent_subj,
    data = email, family = binomial) |>
  tidy()
```

###

Each row tests the null hypothesis that its coefficient is zero, and with **multiple predictors** "each hypothesis test (for each of the explanatory variables) is conditioned on each of the other variables remaining in the model." The p-value of 1.95e-10 on `to_multiple1`, for example, assumes `cc`, `dollar`, and `urgent_subj` are all in the model too.

### Exercise 7

Change the code so that it keeps only the predictors, not the intercept, whose p-value is below 0.05. Render.

```{r}

```

###

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-7-test
#| echo: true
glm(spam ~ to_multiple + cc + dollar + urgent_subj,
    data = email, family = binomial) |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)", p.value < 0.05)
```

###

Three predictors remain, and `cc`, with a p-value of 0.245, is gone. "The very low p-values from the software output tell us that three of the variables (that is, not `cc`) act as statistically discernible predictors in the model at the discernibility level of 0.05, despite the inclusion of any of the other variables."

### Exercise 8

Add a column that divides each estimate by its standard error. Render.

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-8-test
#| echo: true
glm(spam ~ to_multiple + cc + dollar + urgent_subj,
    data = email, family = binomial) |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)", p.value < 0.05) |>
  mutate(ratio = estimate / std.error)
```

###

The new column matches `statistic` exactly: the z statistic counts how many standard errors an estimate sits from zero. The `dollar` estimate, -0.069, looks tiny, but "in units of standard errors (0.02 here), 0.07 is actually quite far from zero, it's all about context!"

Seven of the first ten emails get the same prediction, 0.114. "We'd like to assess the quality of the model," and the chapter's test is this: "if we look at emails that we modeled as having 10% chance of being spam, do we find out 10% of them actually are spam?"

### Exercise 16

Replace the code in that chunk so that it groups the emails into buckets by predicted probability, with breaks at 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, and 0.12. For each bucket, show the number of emails, the average predicted probability, and the observed proportion that are spam, ordered from the lowest prediction to the highest. Render.

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-16
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-16-test
#| echo: true
spam_fit |>
  augment(type.predict = "response") |>
  mutate(bucket = cut(.fitted, breaks = c(0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 1))) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            predicted = mean(.fitted),
            observed = mean(spam == "1"),
            .by = bucket) |>
  arrange(predicted)
```

###

In the biggest bucket, 2,756 emails predicted at 11.3% spam turned out 11.2% spam, which is just what a good model should do. These are the chapter's first steps: "Bucket the observations into groups based on their predicted probabilities," then compute the average predicted and the observed probability for each group.

### Exercise 17

Add the lower and upper ends of a 95% confidence interval for the observed proportion in each bucket, using its standard error. Render.

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-17
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: model-output-and-diagnostics-17-test
#| echo: true
spam_fit |>
  augment(type.predict = "response") |>
  mutate(bucket = cut(.fitted, breaks = c(0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 1))) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            predicted = mean(.fitted),
            observed = mean(spam == "1"),
            .by = bucket) |>
  arrange(predicted) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(observed * (1 - observed) / n),
         lower = observed - 1.96 * se,
         upper = observed + 1.96 * se)
```

###

"We can use the confidence intervals to roughly gauge whether anything might be amiss." Four of the six intervals contain their bucket's average prediction, but in the two buckets predicted at 2% to 8% spam, the whole interval sits below the prediction.

spam_fit |>

###

"Depending on the goal of the research project, you might be inclined to focus on variable importance (through p-values) or you might be inclined to focus on prediction accuracy (through cross-validation)." So far, this tutorial has done the first.

## Cross-validation for prediction error

"The p-value is a probability measure under a setting of no relationship." It tells us whether a variable matters, but "the p-value does not measure how well the model will predict the individual emails (e.g., the accuracy of the model)," which is what **cross-validation** measures.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk with a logistic regression of `spam` on `to_multiple` alone, using `email`. Show every column of the output. Render.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-1-test
#| echo: true
glm(spam ~ to_multiple, data = email, family = binomial) |>
  tidy()
```

###

This is the chapter's smaller model, -2.12 - 1.81 × `to_multiple`, fit to all 3,921 emails. "As with linear regression [...], we compare a smaller logistic regression model to a larger logistic regression model."

### Exercise 2

Replace the code in that chunk so that it creates `email_folds`: `email` with a new column, `fold`, that assigns each email at random to one of four folds of equal size, splitting the spam evenly among them. Set the seed to 470 first. Then count the emails by `fold` and `spam`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-2-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(470)
email_folds <- email |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep(1:4, length.out = n())), .by = spam)

email_folds |>
  count(fold, spam)
```

###

Each fold holds about 980 emails, 91 or 92 of them spam. "Using *k*-fold cross-validation, we can build *k* different models which are used to predict the observations in each of the *k* holdout samples"; the chapter uses four folds and seed 470 too, but a different function, so its folds, and every number that follows, differ slightly from ours, as yours may.

Splitting the spam evenly keeps each fold close to the inbox's 9% spam, so no holdout sample is unusually easy or hard. Every model below is fit to three folds and judged on the fourth.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-12-test
#| echo: true
cv_predict <- function(formula) {
  map(1:4, \(k)
    glm(formula, data = filter(email_folds, fold != k), family = binomial) |>
      augment(newdata = filter(email_folds, fold == k),
              type.predict = "response")) |>
    list_rbind()
}

bind_rows(smaller = cv_predict(spam ~ to_multiple),
          larger = cv_predict(spam ~ to_multiple + attach + winner + format +
                                re_subj + exclaim_mess + number),
          .id = "model") |>
  mutate(predicted_spam = if_else(.fitted > 0.1, "1", "0")) |>
  summarize(count = n(),
            accuracy = mean(spam == predicted_spam),
            notspamTP = mean(predicted_spam[spam == "0"] == "0"),
            spamTP = mean(predicted_spam[spam == "1"] == "1"),
            .by = c(model, fold))
```

###

Eight rows, one for each model and fold, put the trade-off side by side: the larger model's accuracy runs from 0.76 to 0.82, against 0.23 to 0.26 for the smaller one. In fold 4 the larger model caught only 59% of the spam, the kind of fold-to-fold variation a single train-and-test split would hide.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-13-test
#| echo: true
cv_predict <- function(formula) {
  map(1:4, \(k)
    glm(formula, data = filter(email_folds, fold != k), family = binomial) |>
      augment(newdata = filter(email_folds, fold == k),
              type.predict = "response")) |>
    list_rbind()
}

bind_rows(smaller = cv_predict(spam ~ to_multiple),
          larger = cv_predict(spam ~ to_multiple + attach + winner + format +
                                re_subj + exclaim_mess + number),
          .id = "model") |>
  mutate(predicted_spam = if_else(.fitted > 0.1, "1", "0")) |>
  summarize(notspamTP = mean(predicted_spam[spam == "0"] == "0"),
            spamTP = mean(predicted_spam[spam == "1"] == "1"),
            .by = c(model, fold)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(notspamTP, spamTP), names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rate, color = measure)) +
  geom_point()
```

###

The two colors cross: the smaller model sits high on `spamTP` and low on `notspamTP`, and the larger model brings the two together, between 59% and 85%. The four folds of each model land close together, so the difference between the models is not an accident of one split.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation-for-prediction-error-14-test
#| echo: true
cv_predict <- function(formula) {
  map(1:4, \(k)
    glm(formula, data = filter(email_folds, fold != k), family = binomial) |>
      augment(newdata = filter(email_folds, fold == k),
              type.predict = "response")) |>
    list_rbind()
}

bind_rows(smaller = cv_predict(spam ~ to_multiple),
          larger = cv_predict(spam ~ to_multiple + attach + winner + format +
                                re_subj + exclaim_mess + number),
          .id = "model") |>
  mutate(predicted_spam = if_else(.fitted > 0.1, "1", "0")) |>
  summarize(notspamTP = mean(predicted_spam[spam == "0"] == "0"),
            spamTP = mean(predicted_spam[spam == "1"] == "1"),
            .by = c(model, fold)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(notspamTP, spamTP), names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate") |>
  mutate(model = fct_relevel(if_else(model == "smaller",
                                     "Smaller: 1 predictor",
                                     "Larger: 7 predictors"),
                             "Smaller: 1 predictor"),
         measure = if_else(measure == "spamTP",
                           "Spam caught (spamTP)",
                           "Real email let through (notspamTP)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rate, color = measure)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = interaction(measure, fold)), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Cross-Validated Spam Predictions from Two Logistic Models",
       subtitle = "The larger model catches less spam (69% vs. 97%)\nbut lets through far more real email (79% vs. 17%)",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Proportion Predicted Correctly",
       color = NULL,
       caption = "3,921 emails in four folds, each predicted by a model fit to the other three; spam if predicted probability > 10%\nSource: openintro package, David Diez's Gmail account, January to March 2012") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

###

"However, it is not true that adding variables will always lead to better predictions, as correlated or noise variables may dampen the signal from the set of variables that truly predict the status." Cross-validation is how you find out, because every point on the plot comes from emails the model never saw.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 26: Inference for logistic regression](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inf-model-logistic.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned to read the standard errors, z statistics, and p-values of a logistic regression, to check a model by comparing its predicted probabilities with what actually happened, and to compare two models with cross-validation, using emails from one inbox, some of them spam.

The chapter's own summary, in the authors' words:

> Throughout the text, we have presented a modern view to introduction to statistics. Earlier, we presented graphical techniques which communicated relationships across multiple variables. We also used modeling to formalize the relationships. In [Chapter 26] we considered inferential claims on models which include many variables used to predict the probability of the outcome being a success. We continue to emphasize the importance of experimental design in making conclusions about research claims. In particular, recall that variability can come from different sources (e.g., random sampling vs. random allocation, see [the figure on sampling and assignment in Chapter 2]).
>
> As you might guess, this text has only scratched the surface of the world of statistical analyses that can be applied to different datasets. In particular, to do justice to the topic, the linear models and generalized linear models we have introduced can each be covered with their own course or book. Hierarchical models, alternative methods for fitting parameters (e.g., Ridge Regression or LASSO), and advanced computational methods applied to multivariable models (e.g., permuting the response variable? one explanatory variable? all the explanatory variables?) are all beyond the scope of this book. However, your successful understanding of the ideas we have covered has set you up perfectly to move on to a higher level of statistical modeling and inference. Enjoy!

For the next step, read [*Tidy Modeling with R*](https://www.tmwr.org/) by Max Kuhn and Julia Silge, the guide to **tidymodels**, the packages the chapter uses for its folds and models. For cross-validation, ridge regression, and the LASSO, which the chapter leaves for later, read [*An Introduction to Statistical Learning*](https://www.statlearning.com/) by Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani.

spam_fit <- glm(spam ~ to_multiple + cc + dollar + urgent_subj,
                data = email, family = binomial)

```{r}
spam_fit |>
  augment(type.predict = "response") |>
  mutate(bucket = cut(.fitted, breaks = c(0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 1))) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            predicted = mean(.fitted),
            observed = mean(spam == "1"),
            .by = bucket) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(observed * (1 - observed) / n),
         lower = observed - 1.96 * se,
         upper = observed + 1.96 * se) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = predicted, y = observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 0.35), ylim = c(0, 0.35)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted and Observed Spam Rates",
       subtitle = "Observed spam rates track the predictions, except between 2% and 8%",
       x = "Average Predicted Probability of Spam",
       y = "Observed Proportion of Spam",
       size = "Emails",
       caption = "3,921 emails in six buckets; bars are 95% confidence intervals\nSource: openintro, David Diez's Gmail, Jan.-Mar. 2012")
```

"We also used modeling to formalize the relationships." Your two plots check one model two ways: the first asks whether its probabilities are honest, the second whether its predictions hold up on emails it never saw.
